questions.question: A paper says a multi-agent design is better. What does the lesson say to ask before accepting the claim?
options: Which benchmark, split, baseline, and cost were measured
How many agents appear in the architecture diagram
Whether the paper uses a recent model name
Whether the conclusion uses the word coordination
questions.explanation: A result is interpretable only with its benchmark and split, a relevant baseline, and the cost; trial count and task diversity also shape confidence. Counting agents in a diagram does not show whether performance improves or generalizes.

questions.question: What does MultiAgentBench/MARBLE use to track partial progress during a task?
options: A model's self-reported confidence
Only a final binary success label
Milestone-based key performance indicators
The number of tools in each agent
questions.explanation: MARBLE tracks partial progress with milestone-based KPIs, so a task can earn credit for completed intermediate goals before full success. A final binary label loses that trajectory information.

questions.question: A multimodal coordination system performs no better than a random policy on COMMA. What does the lesson recommend?
options: Treat it as a warning and measure before claiming coordination gains
Increase the number of model parameters without retesting
Assume any multimodal model is better than random
Remove the random baseline from future comparisons
questions.explanation: If a multimodal system only matches random on COMMA, the result warns that its coordination ability has not been demonstrated. Removing the random baseline would hide the comparison needed to support a gain claim.

questions.question: What lesson does MedAgentBoard contribute to multi-agent design?
options: More agents dominate single-model systems in every medical task
Multi-agent may not beat one model without useful decomposition
Coordination overhead disappears when roles are named
A benchmark should exclude single-model baselines
questions.explanation: MedAgentBoard finds that multi-agent systems do not automatically beat a single model; task decomposition helps when subtasks are separable, while coordination overhead can outweigh specialization. Merely naming roles does not remove that overhead.

questions.question: A public benchmark is close to saturated and may appear in training data. What evaluation step can reveal overfitting?
options: Compare performance on seen and held-out task splits
Remove task identifiers from the results table
Report only the best seen-task score
Use more agents on the same seen examples
questions.explanation: Compare performance on seen and held-out tasks; a large gap can signal memorization or contamination rather than generalization. Reporting only the best seen split selects the conditions most favorable to the model.

questions.question: A new coordination benchmark has high raw accuracy but a large cost per task. What should the report include?
options: The highest-scoring run without trial count
Cost alongside accuracy and wall-clock time
The model family but not the task split
Only the final answer and agent count
questions.explanation: Accuracy needs cost per task and wall-clock time alongside it, since a quality gain may require much more compute or time. Reporting only the final answer omits whether the approach is viable for its intended use.
